Seminar Title:

Evaluating the Dynamic and Thermodynamic Environment Accompanying North Indian Ocean Tropical Cyclones through Composite Analysis

Seminar Type:

Department:

Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Speaker Name:

Speaker Type:

ER-303, Department of Earth and Atmospheric Sciences

Jagabandhu Panda

Abstract:

Tropical cyclones (TCs) over the North Indian Ocean (NIO) pose substantial hazards through strong winds, extreme rainfall, coastal inundation, and storm surges. Despite their relatively low frequency, NIO TCs exhibit considerable variability in track behaviour, lifespan, and structural evolution, while the environmental factors associated with these characteristics play a vital role. This work investigates such aspects through climatological and composite analysis of observational and reanalysis datasets, complemented by numerical simulations using the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model and three-dimensional variational (3DVAR) assimilation of satellite-derived scatterometer winds. It employs a basin-specific, angle-based classification scheme, which was developed and optimized using 136 NIO TCs by reducing the turning-angle threshold from 45&deg to 30&deg and refining the criteria for identifying distinct track types. Extreme turning-angle analysis revealed seasonal variability, with stronger turning angles during the post-monsoon season. Composite analysis indicated that large-scale dynamical circulation provides the primary environmental framework for recurvature, while atmospheric moisture and convective activity modulate the associated environment. A lifespan-based analysis adopted for distinguished long (LDC), moderate (MDC), and short-duration cyclones (SDC) and revealed contrasting atmospheric and oceanic conditions across varying categories. LDCs were associated with persistent cyclonic vorticity, upper-level divergence, relatively moderate vertical wind shear, and a moist mid-troposphere, together with sustained oceanic heat content and upper-ocean stratification, particularly over the Bay of Bengal (BOB). However, SDCs exhibited stronger wind shear, lower mid-tropospheric humidity, weaker vortex organization, and more rapid oceanic cooling. The structural characteristics of BOB TCs were examined using WRF simulated outputs, with and without scatterometer-wind assimilation. Data assimilation generally improved the representation of maximum sustained wind, minimum sea-level pressure, track, and dynamical structure, particularly for severe and highly intensified cyclones, but had a comparatively limited influence on thermodynamic fields. The corresponding analysis of Arabian Sea TCs also revealed pronounced seasonal differences, with post-monsoon storms exhibiting more organized vortex and wind structures and distinct moisture and diabatic-heating distributions. Together, these results provide an integrated, basin-specific assessment of TC track behaviour, lifespan, and structure, demonstrating the importance of considering sub-basin and seasonal variability, and establish the value and limitations of scatterometer-wind assimilation for improving their representation in numerical simulations over the NIO basin.
